Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy.
Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.
Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed.
Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before.
Fuel, light and water charges also saw a considerable acceleration, increasing 3.4% compared to last month's 0.8%.
Following the release, the Nikkei 225 index was down 2.1%, while the 10-year JGB yield fell 2 basis points to 2.805%.
Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports.
The October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan.
"The BOJ is likely to look through the temporary weakness in 3Q GDP and focus instead on underlying inflation and wage dynamics," Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research, wrote in a Monday note.
On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament that the central bank was also "mindful" of the weak yen and rising crude prices, saying that these could hurt households' real income and weigh on consumption more than expected.

VOO is a passive fund that tracks the S&P 500. It buys a stock only after S&P Dow Jones Indices adds that company to the index, and Vanguard’s managers don’t pick IPOs or make calls on hot debuts.

Reuters, CNBC, Bloomberg and Business Insider reported the decision as a refusal to fast-track mega IPOs such as SpaceX, and Ars Technica reported that it also blocks early entry for OpenAI and Anthropic. Starting 12 months from the November 19, 2026 debut, the index committee can’t consider Anthropic until late 2027.

But tax liability insurance is less familiar and equally useful in asset management where it can be deployed to vastly speed up closing a fund for a minimal cost.
When a fund has an uncertain lifespan
Alternative investment funds often have a fixed lifespan. They spend the first few years buying illiquid assets and then spend the remaining years selling them off.
However, fund liabilities can have a long, uncertain lifespan, making their wind-down difficult and slow. Contingent tax liabilities can have a long tail of six or more years due to statutes of limitations in certain US jurisdictions.
Hedge funds can often give investors their money back regularly because they hold assets that are easy to sell based on investor demand for capital. But private equity funds, credit funds, infrastructure funds and real estate funds generally consist of illiquid assets that need to be sold opportunistically and generally can’t provide investors with full liquidity.
As a result, private equity fund managers will frequently advertise an expected investment period and expected fund lifespan – without making any assurances. But investors can be reluctant to invest without an indication of when they’ll see a return on their money.
Fund managers earn performance bonuses (carried interest) based on how quickly they return cash to investors. To hit these targets and wrap up an aging fund, managers sometimes sell their remaining assets to a new, secondary fund, often called a continuation fund backed by a different group of investors or a subset of the original investors.
However, fund managers struggle to control how long a fund’s financial obligations last, and buyers who take over existing funds usually don’t want to inherit old debts and risks. In the investment world, tax liabilities are especially problematic because they can linger for a very long time.
Tax liabilities, a long-tail risk
Certain tax liabilities can, of course, be eliminated by paying the appropriate tax authority. But contingent tax risks relating to uncertain positions taken by the fund can have a significantly longer tail.
In the US, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) generally has three years to audit a tax return, but this extends to six years if you substantially underreport your income. Ongoing disputes can drag on much longer if the IRS asks for more time to finish an audit or there are court delays. This is when tax insurance can be an alternative asset manager’s best friend.
The solution: tax insurance
Tax insurance is a rapidly growing tool for managing tax risk but is particularly useful for alternative asset managers, who can use it to close down funds sooner without having to worry about investor holdbacks or clawbacks.
It shifts the financial risk of a tax dispute from a company, funds or investors to an insurer. Tax insurance generally covers potential losses for additional taxes, interest, penalties, and defense costs.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to classify workers as independent contractors rather than their employees, who have more legal protections and can cost more.
The Department of Labor scrapped a rule adopted during the administration of former President Joe Biden, and replaced it with a legal test favored by business groups.
The new rule could lower costs for companies in a range of industries, including trucking, healthcare, retail sales and app-based transportation and delivery services such as Uber, that rely heavily on contractors. Such companies routinely face lawsuits accusing them of misclassifying workers to save money, which they deny.
The Labor Department said the 2024 rule was legally flawed and that the new test creates a clearer standard for businesses and workers to follow.
“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in a statement.
The rule will take effect in January, 60 days after it is formally published.
New Rule Focuses on Control
The Biden-era rule had established factors for determining whether a worker should be classified as an employee or contractor under federal wage law, and any one of them could tip the scales toward employee status.
The rule finalized on Thursday instead focuses on whether workers are under a company’s control or have the opportunity for profit or loss based on their own initiative or investment.
Employees can cost businesses up to 30% more, according to several surveys, because they are entitled to the minimum wage, overtime pay, unemployment insurance, reimbursements for expenses and other protections not afforded to contractors.
Worker classification has been one of the most contentious employment-related issues over the last decade, and trade groups lobbied heavily to repeal the 2024 rule after an effort by Republicans in Congress to block it stalled.
The Biden-era rule had replaced a regulation adopted during Trump’s first term that said workers who own their own businesses or can work for competing companies — such as a driver who works for Uber and Lyft — can be treated as contractors. The new rule is similar to that standard.
Supporters of the Biden-era rule have said misclassification of workers is rampant in some industries, and that repealing the rule would allow employers to strip workers of basic legal protections.

The US government was warned four years ago that security weaknesses in national telecommunications networks had created a “perilous” situation and left the country vulnerable to foreign spies, but it fought to keep a report detailing those concerns secret and didn’t address its findings, according to interviews and documents reviewed by Bloomberg News.
A June 2022 report commissioned by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency concluded that US telecommunications networks contained “major structural vulnerabilities” that had created national security risks. “The fact that US national networks can be readily compromised from anywhere in the world is not yet widely understood,” states the report.
The report, which was disclosed as part of a lawsuit and reviewed by Bloomberg, was produced more than two years before revelations that a suspected Chinese hacking group known as Salt Typhoon had breached at least nine major U.S. telecommunications and broadband providers, including Verizon, AT&T and Lumen Technologies. The intruders targeted the phones of top politicians — including then presidential candidate Donald Trump — in what US officials described as the one of the worst cyber espionage cases in the recent history.
The Salt Typhoon hackers used an obscure telecom protocol called SS7, or Signaling System 7, which was one of the vulnerabilities identified in the report, for some early reconnaissance efforts, said a former US official familiar with the breaches. But they didn’t exploit it to gain access to US telecommunications networks, according to the person, and a second former official familiar with the matter. Both spoke on the condition they not be identified because of the sensitivity of the matter.
CISA withheld the report from public release for four years and resisted congressional pressure to publish it. Still, Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon whose office was briefed on the report’s findings in 2023 and pushed for its release, said it advocated an overhaul that could have helped shore up US networks.
“Had this report been made public when it was first written in 2022, Congress would have had ample time to require mandatory cybersecurity standards for phone companies, in time to prevent the Salt Typhoon hacks,” Wyden said in a statement last year. In a statement to Bloomberg this week, he said, “It is totally inexcusable that CISA stonewalled releasing this report for four years, while adversaries were spying on Americans.”
After fighting against its release, CISA provided a redacted version of the report to Washington-based Electronic Privacy Information Center, which sued to get it under the Freedom of Information Act. The details of the report haven’t been previously reported.

Top officials in Florida this week approved some significant changes to the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund’s reimbursement contract, potentially allowing property insurers to recover much more in living expenses when homeowners are displaced after a storm.
The Florida Cabinet, made up of the governor, the state’s chief financial officer, the attorney general and the agriculture commissioner, voted Nov. 17 to change the definition of “additional living expenses” for which the Cat Fund will reimburse carriers.
Current contract language limits Cat Fund living expense reimbursement to no more than 40% of the insured value of a home. It also notes that fair rental value, loss of rents, or business interruption losses are not covered by the FHCF.
The proposed new wording appears to give insurers more wiggle room: Additional living expenses would be defined simply as “reasonable and necessary temporary living expenses incurred by the policyholder that are beyond the policyholder’s normal living expenses when a covered event renders the residential structure where the policyholder resides unlivable or is prohibited from use by a civil authority.”
Florida Statute 215.555(2)(d) now requires the 40% limit. The proposed change would keep the reference to the statute in the contract, but would remove the specific wording about 40% of insured value of the home. That suggests that Florida lawmakers at the upcoming 2027 legislative session may be asked to consider removing the percentage requirement.
Another section of the proposed contract notes that the Cat Fund’s governing body, the State Board of Administration, “may require at anytime a company to submit a proof of loss report for any covered event in a contract year prior to reimbursement of losses for a specific covered event.”
If finalized, the new contract would be in effect from June 1, 2027 to May 30, 2028.
A bulletin posted by the Florida Insurance Council, an association that represents some 300 businesses, explained that the next step is for the Cat Fund to publish a final version of the rule. Then, stakeholders can request a hearing and submit comments. If no hearing is requested, the rule will become final.

A federal judge ruled President Donald Trump can proceed with his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times, giving a boost to his ongoing cases against the press.
US District Judge Steven Merryday in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday denied a request by one of the world’s most prominent news organizations to dismiss the case, which the president filed last year. Trump accused the news outlet of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election.
The judge dismissed two claims in the suit and narrowed four others. The surviving claims relate to statements accusing Trump of tax fraud, tax evasion, money laundering or related criminal conduct.
Merryday, appointed by former President George H.W. Bush, ruled Trump sufficiently alleged that the Times had acted with “actual malice,” meaning its journalists knew the statements were false or acted with “reckless disregard for the truth.” The actual malice standard — a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation — was established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.
However, Thursday’s ruling significantly narrows the case by eliminating more than two dozen challenged statements, mostly from Times articles.
The ruling does not find that the New York Times defamed Trump, but it holds that the allegations are sufficient to survive the newspaper’s motion to dismiss. The decision means the case is now on track for a potential trial.
Merryday held that the disputed Times statements accuse the president of tax crimes without an “explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts.”
“Knowing of the necessity for that opinion but failing to procure that opinion is a fine example of the purposeful avoidance of the truth,” the judge said.
The New York Times did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. A representative of Trump’s legal team also did not immediately respond.
The lawsuit is one of several filed by Trump against the media since the start of his second term. A $10 billion defamation suit Trump filed against the Wall Street Journal was thrown out by a different judge in a ruling that barred him from refiling it. The British Broadcasting Corp. lost its move to dismiss a $10 billion suit brought by Trump.
The Times could appeal the ruling. For now, the decision sets up the case for a potential trial in which opposing views of the First Amendment’s press protections are expected to feature heavily.
Trump sued in September 2025, alleging the Times tarnished his reputation with three articles and a book written by its journalists. The Times argued the reporting was accurate.

Touring the world’s largest wildlife crossing, Beth Pratt stepped carefully through freshly planted native vegetation and held up her hand for silence.
“Hear that? We’re listening to birdsong right now, on top of one of the busiest freeways in the U.S.!” a beaming Pratt, one of the project’s leaders, said excitedly. “That makes my heart glad.”
The warbling was the latest sign that the bridge, spanning U.S. 101 and a feeder road about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of downtown Los Angeles, is already in use by animals ahead of the official Dec. 2 opening ceremony.
Just two weeks earlier, motion-sensor cameras captured a lone coyote believed to be the first mammal to make the trek safely across. Days after that momentous crossing, three juvenile coyotes were seen on camera playing in the brush beneath the 10-foot (3-meter) sound-dampening walls that line the span.
“They don’t care about ribbon cuttings,” laughed Pratt, president of the nonprofit Wildlife Crossing Fund.
About 300,000 cars a day travel that stretch of the 101 in Agoura Hills, a small city surrounded by a patchwork of protected wildland that the new crossing will connect. Fencing along the freeway funnels animals to the crossing.
The bridge, with a landscape that’s indistinguishable from surrounding hillsides, stretches 1,250 feet (380 meters) in two sections over the roadways to give animals hemmed in by urban sprawl a safe path to the nearby Santa Monica Mountains and beyond.
It is named the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing for the late philanthropist whose foundation donated $25 million toward the $114 million total budget. Software carries IBM's profits

Showing how much the business has bounced back, software revenue grew 9% year over year in constant currency (a measure that removes exchange-rate moves) in the third quarter. The American Property Casualty Insurance Association is one of eight organizations pushing federal lawmakers to rethink and fine tune legislation regarding consumer choice when it comes to vehicle repair.
The matter, they said, is important because current limitations on just how and where vehicles are fixed has increased the cost of repairs because parts in some cases are limited to more expensive original equipment manufacturer (OEM) options, and access to vehicle-generated diagnostics, data, and software is restricted – especially when it comes to modern vehicles.
A federal standard is needed to ensure consumers have the right to choose who repairs their vehicles and what parts are used.
“According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, over the last five years in the absence of a federal right to repair, vehicle repair costs increased over 40%,” said the groups signing the letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Along with the APCIA, others include the Auto Care Association, CAR Coalition, MEMA Aftermarket Suppliers, Commercial Vehicle Solutions Network, National Federation of Independent Business, National Independent Automobile Dealers Association, and Preventative Automotive Maintenance Association.
They said they’d like to see more provisions within the Right to Equitable and Professional Auto Industry Repair (REPAIR) Act (HR 1566) included in any legislation. Provisions of the REPAIR Act were included earlier this year within another piece of legislation, the Motor Vehicle Modernization Act of 2026 (HR 7389), passed by a House committee. However, REPAIR Act sponsor Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) has said the legislation passed “does not fully reflect the original REPAIR Act and fails to protect consumers, independent repair shops, and aftermarket manufacturers.”
The organizations signing the letter to House leaders apparently agree. The MVMA Act included “repair provisions based largely on limited voluntary memoranda of understanding developed more than a decade ago. These agreements fail to meet automotive repair marketplace needs in 2026,” they said.
“Recent developments underscore why voluntary industry policies are not enough,” the groups continued, adding that General Motors recently released its position that it “strictly prohibits” use of non-OEM parts for repair.
“This guidance effectively restricts consumer choice and forces the use of more expensive OEM parts,” the groups said. “GM’s position statement is illustrative of a broader trend: Several other automakers, including Ford, Honda, and Nissan, have rolled out similar restrictions.

Wall Street’s biggest banks have spent the past several quarters handing more cash back to shareholders, and all four names below raised their quarterly dividends along the way. For retirees, the appeal is income that keeps growing from companies that clear the Federal Reserve’s capital hurdles, pay out a modest slice of earnings, and still have cash left for heavy buybacks. All four yield in the low single digits, so the case for them rests on dividend safety and growth.
Wells Fargo: A Rebuilt Dividend Closing In on Its Old Peak
Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) yields 2.24% at a share price of $81.32. The quarterly dividend rose from $0.45 to $0.50 starting with the third-quarter payment, which puts the forward annual rate at $2 per share.
Retirees should know the full history. Wells Fargo cut its dividend in 2020, from $0.51 to $0.10 a quarter. Since then, it has rebuilt the payout one step at a time: $0.20 in 2021, $0.30 by late 2022, $0.35 in 2023, $0.40 in 2024, $0.45 in 2025, and $0.50 now. The current rate sits just below the pre-cut level.
One rule applies to all four banks. Big-bank dividends operate inside limits set by regulators. Cindy O'Laughlin, pictured speaking to reporters in May 2024, will lead Missouri's education department as interim commissioner beginning Dec. 1 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, will lead Missouri’s Department of Elementary and Secondary Education as interim commissioner of education beginning Dec. 1.
The State Board of Education voted 6-1 to appoint O’Laughlin in a closed meeting Friday morning. It will continue its search for a permanent commissioner, aiming to hire a permanent commissioner by June.
“I recognize that this is an interim role, and my responsibility is to provide steady leadership while the board continues its search for a permanent commissioner,” O’Laughlin told The Independent Friday afternoon. “I have told the board I will not be vying for that position. But that doesn’t mean we should stand still.”
The board has “important work underway to improve accountability, establish clear goals and focus on student achievement,” she said. The department is currently working on an A-F grading system for public schools requested by Gov. Mike Kehoe, drawing criticism from educators who fear schools’ reputation will be impacted by a scoring system they see as flawed.
“I am ready to roll up my sleeves and get to work,” O’Laughlin said. “Our kids deserve nothing less.”
She will replace Lisa Sireno, who has served as interim commissioner since Oct. 21 following the resignation of Stacey Preis.
Missouri state education board selects interim commissioner amid leadership shakeup
The announcement came after months of rumors that O’Laughlin was being eyed for the position. As word circulated more widely in the past month, the state board’s inbox filled with angry emails and questions about her qualifications.
Wheaton school Superintendent Alyssa Kennedy was among those who opposed O’Laughlin’s possible appointment, sharing her letter to the board in a Facebook post.
“I respectfully urge the Board not to make this appointment based on political alignment or a predetermined outcome,” she wrote. “If the Board is considering Senator O’Laughlin, I urge you to carefully examine whether her experience and policy positions align with the responsibilities and public mission of this office.”
State law requires the commissioner to “possess an educational attainment and breadth of experience in the administration of public education.”
O’Laughlin’s Senate biography says she has experience “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.” The Independent could not find record of her work in these positions.
A resume provided by O’Laughlin shows that she worked in a variety of positions in Northeast Missouri, including as co-founder and administrator of an unnamed Christian school and daycare in Macon, prior to opening a concrete business in 1993. In the document, she cites work in the legislature as a key part of her achievements in education.
O’Laughlin chaired the Senate Education Committee from 2020 to 2022, telling public school advocates that she hoped to work with them and that she was not an expert, as The Independent reported in 2021.

The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.
The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA.
The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.

Just two Republicans — Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor.

Roberta Groner had what she calls “a rocky road” for the year leading up to the New York City Marathon on November 1.
In her previous three attempts at the marathon, during which she had hoped to run an Olympic Marathon Trials qualifying time (2:37), she had racked up three DNFs in a row.
She was in great shape for the Valencia Marathon in December 2025, having just run 1:12:21 for the half marathon, and she thought she might be in shape to better her lifetime PR in the marathon, which is 2:29:09, from 2019, when she was 41. Her conservative goal was getting the Trials time.
But a warm day in Spain—about 75 degrees—and a brain lock about translating kilometers into miles caused her to step off the course late in the race. Her coach, Devon Martin, of the Central Park Track Club, still rues that one. “She had no idea she had seven minutes to spare at mile 18,” Martin said.
Two weeks later, Groner hopped in the Marathon Project in Arizona. Martin had tried to convince her not to. Sure enough, her legs hadn’t recovered from the hard miles in Valencia, and she dropped out there, too.
Then came Grandma’s Marathon in June in Duluth, Minnesota. Groner felt off. She later realized that her body was adjusting to starting hormone replacement therapy for perimenopause symptoms. Another DNF.
By the time she got to New York City, her hometown race, Groner—a former nurse who is now a full-time coach with Central Park Track Club—was uncharacteristically a basket case.
“I had to fight some mental demons, especially the week before,” she said. “My coach was probably like, ‘Oh, I can't handle her.’”
Groner ran with the elite women, always a small group in New York, which leaves those who can’t keep pace with the strange sensation of running a big-city marathon alone. She was well behind the leaders, running side-by-side with Steph Bruce for the first 17 miles, before Bruce fell back. Groner spent the next 9 miles with her eyes scanning the distance for any women she could pick off on the way to the finish.
She passed a handful of runners in the final stretch and finished 22nd in 2:35:55, her third Olympic Trials qualifier. She’ll be 50 when the race goes off in St. Louis. Dot McMahan of Michigan, who has qualified for her sixth trials, will be 51.
“I was able to race and compete, which was great,” Groner said. “And yeah, it wasn't my fastest New York, but I was really happy with the performance. Knowing that my faster days could be done, I still want to race really well. To be able to pass a few people at the end. I’ll give it an A.”
But are her fastest days really behind her? Groner doesn’t necessarily think so. And she’s not backing off her goals just because she’s in her late 40s.
She had a decade away from running when her three sons—now 23, 20, and 19—were growing up, which makes her feel like a younger runner than she is. When Cameron Balser arrived at New York City Hall at 11:45 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 20, 2026, he set a new speed record for the Trans America Run, a route stretching from San Francisco, California, on the West Coast, to New York City on the East Coast and covering 3,067 miles (4,935 kilometers).
He’d been running on the route, affectionately called the “TransAm,” for 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes, and he was joined by a large crowd on the streets of New York City to celebrate his accomplishment.
When Balser left the San Francisco City Hall at 5:00 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time, on October 10, he was chasing Pete Kostelnick’s record from 2016. Kostelnick ran between the city halls in 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes. With seemingly the tightest of margins for a run of this length, Balser broke Kostelnick’s time by 13 hours and 45 minutes.
He’d covered more than 140,000 feet of elevation gain while traversing across California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and finally New York, and averaged 73.61 miles per day. Running over mountains, through deserts and prairies, and everything in between, Basler’s consistency over all types of terrain was impressive, both with his efficient crew and his steady pace.
Across the Country
The 35-year-old Indiana native named his run “Breaking 42,” making his intentions to run farther than Kostelnick’s 72.56-mile daily average clear from the start. Winter weather delays in the Rockies complicated Balser’s plans early on, including a forced early stop due to rain that made a dirt road impassable for support-vehicle access and snow at the high point of his route, Cameron Pass, in Colorado.
With remarkable consistency, Balser broke his 15- to 16-hour days into five-mile segments, taking in around 800 calories at each crew stop to keep his energy levels up. He aimed to run every uphill stretch to finish each day’s mileage as efficiently as possible.
Once out of the Colorado mountains, Balser went on to surge across the prairies, cranking out 75-mile days through the flatter terrain of the Midwest and East Coast as he closed in on New York. Throughout the route, he was joined by friends and fans, and he kept a live tracker available for anyone who wanted to share miles with him.
Unlike a fixed trail fastest known time where the route is defined, the Trans America Run record is defined by its endpoints — the San Francisco City Hall and New York City Hall — and Balser’s crew spent months studying Kostelnick’s 2016 blueprint, even joking on social media that they were “sick and tired of studying [his] route/record.”
Prior record holder Kostelnick cheered Balser on throughout his attempt. A couple of days before Balser’s finish, he quipped on social media: “It’s always humbling to see a record you put so (damn) much into get broken, but I’ve learned it also requires genuine appreciation for the person willing to chase your ghost. To really recognize them, especially when they’ve done it the right way. San Francisco to NYC. Showing happiness over clicks. Give us more of that, Cameron.”
On the final night, Balser was joined by several dozen runners for the last 11 miles in from the George Washington Bridge. With only a mile left, he clearly relished the cheers from onlookers, stating calmly, “That was a good run.” He walked the final mile to the finish, smiling under the New York City lights.
